rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report cited in Rūḥ al-Maʿānī names the youths مكسلمينا, يمليخا, مرطولس, ثيبونس, دردونس, كفاشيطيطوس, and منطنواسيس; it calls the seventh a shepherd and the dog قطمير.
rows.anchor: على ما صح عن ابن عباس مكسلمينا ويمليخا ومرطولس وثيبونس ودردونس وكفاشيطيطوس ومنطنواسيس وهو الراعي والكلب اسمه قطمير

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: A report attributed to ʿAlī divides six named youths between the king’s right and left, leaves the shepherd unnamed, and names the dog قطمير.
rows.anchor: وهؤلاء أصحاب يساره، وكان يستشير الستة والسابع الراعي ولم يذكر في هذه الرواية اسمه وذكر فيها أن اسم كلبهم قطمير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī questions the attribution of this elaborate report to ʿAlī; it appears in al-Thaʿlabī and al-Daylamī, the latter as a raised report.
rows.anchor: وفي صحة نسبة هذه الرواية لعلي كرم الله وجهه مقال

rows.speaker: الحافظ ابن حجر
rows.claim: Ibn Ḥajar says the youths’ names have many variant pronunciations and cannot be confidently fixed; al-Baḥr likewise calls them foreign and weakly transmitted.
rows.anchor: وذكر الحافظ ابن حجر في شرح البخاري أن في النطق بأسمائهم اختلافا كثيرا

rows.speaker: السيوطي
rows.claim: Al-Suyūṭī says al-Ṭabarānī transmitted the Ibn ʿAbbās naming report in al-Awsaṭ with a sound chain; the report in al-Durr al-manthūr is the same one.
rows.anchor: ذكر العلامة السيوطي في حواشي البيضاوي أن الطبراني روى ذلك عن ابن عباس في معجمه الأوسط بإسناده صحيح

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم
rows.claim: A report from Ibn ʿAbbās attributes to the Prophet the statement that the Companions of the Cave are helpers of the Mahdī.
rows.anchor: أخرج ابن مردويه عن ابن عباس قال قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم

rows.speaker: الصادق عليه السلام
rows.claim: A report says seven Companions of the Cave will join the Qāʾim alongside figures including Joshua, Abū Dujāna, al-Miqdād, and Mālik al-Ashtar as helpers and judges.
rows.anchor: قال الصادق عليه السلام يخرج للقائم عليه السلام من ظهر الكعبة سبعة وعشرين رجلا من قوم موسى

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب عليه السلام
rows.claim: An account from ʿAlī says a person swearing by God may make an exception for forty days, recalling the Prophet’s delayed answer to Jewish questioners after he omitted “if God wills.”
rows.anchor: قال إذا حلف رجل بالله فله ثنياها إلى أربعين يوما وذلك أن قوما من اليهود سألوا النبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī defines thunyā as an exception and says related reports suggest a decisive oath; whether an exception can qualify an already binding oath is left to jurisprudence.
rows.anchor: الثنيا بالضم فالسكون مقصورا اسم الاستثناء وفي هذا المعنى روايات أخر عن الصادقين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cave story circulated in detailed reports from al-Qummī, Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrima, Mujāhid, Ibn Isḥāq, Wahb ibn Munabbih, and al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr, among others.
rows.anchor: وردت قصة الكهف مفصلة كاملة في عدة روايات عن الصحابة والتابعين وأئمه أهل البيت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The transmitted accounts disagree even on major features, while reports about dates, rulers, lineage, appearance, names, and the title أصحاب الرقيم diverge still more.
rows.anchor: من الاختلاف في متونها بحيث لا تكاد تتفق في جهة بارزه من جهات القصة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One cause is the story’s prominence among People of the Book: Quraysh learned it from them, and its Christian images and monuments spread it widely, so communities reshaped it to fit their beliefs.
rows.anchor: أن القصة مما اعتنت به أهل الكتاب كما يستفاد من رواياتها أن قريشا تلقتها عنهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second cause is Muslims’ broad collection of outside reports, especially through converts such as Wahb ibn Munabbih and Kaʿb al-Aḥbār; later transmitters treated such material as prophetic reports.
rows.anchor: اختلط بهم قوم من علماء أهل الكتاب دخلوا في الإسلام كوهب بن منبه وكعب الأحبار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾān selects key lessons that serve guidance instead of supplying a complete historical account; it is a book of guidance, not history.
rows.anchor: فما كتاب الله بكتاب تاريخ وإنما هو كتاب هدى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾānic narrative first shows the youths’ truth-bearing withdrawal and long sleep, then their awakening and exchange that exposes them, and finally their discovery and the mosque built over them.
rows.anchor: أورد أولا شطرا من محاورتهم يشير إلى معنى قيامهم لله وثباتهم على كلمة الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾān omits names, ancestry, birth, upbringing, occupations, social standing, dates, rulers, cities, persecutors, and the dog’s identity because guidance does not depend on them; historians and early exegetes filled these gaps, producing divergent accounts.
rows.anchor: إلى غير ذلك من الأمور التي لا يتوقف غرض الهداية على العلم بشيء منها كما يتوقف عليه غرض البحث التاريخي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The youths lived amid idol worship and were persecuted for their informed monotheistic faith; God increased their guidance, knowledge, and wisdom and strengthened their hearts against fear.
rows.anchor: فتية نشأوا في مجتمع مشرك لا يرى إلا عبادة الأوثان فتسرب في المجتمع دين التوحيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seeing that remaining would force them to conceal truth or conform to idolatry, the youths chose to affirm God as Lord of heaven and earth, reject other gods as false, and withdraw to the cave trusting in divine mercy and guidance.
rows.anchor: علموا أن سبيلهم أن يقوموا على التوحيد ورفض الشرك ثم اعتزال القوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The narrative presents the youths sleeping in the cave with their dog for the stated long period, protected by the cave’s position and God’s care.
rows.anchor: ثم دخلوا الكهف واستقروا على فجوة منه وكلبهم باسط ذراعيه بالوصيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After 309 years God raised the youths to show how He had rescued them; they awoke disoriented, and some guessed they had slept a day or part of one while others deferred to God’s knowledge.
rows.anchor: بعثهم بعد هذا الدهر الطويل وهو ثلاثمائة وتسع سنين من يوم دخلوا الكهف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because they were hungry, the youths sent one with their silver to find wholesome food and instructed him to act discreetly, fearing stoning or forced return to their religion.
rows.anchor: فإنكم جياع وليتلطف الذاهب منكم إلى المدينة في مسيره إليها وشرائه الطعام ولا يشعرن بكم أحدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God allowed their discovery after the persecuting generation and its rule had passed; the new population, dominated by monotheists and disputing resurrection, would receive a sign of it.
rows.anchor: القوم الذين اعتزلوهم وفارقوهم يوم دخلوا الكهف قد انقرضوا وذهب الله بهم وبملكهم وملتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The messenger expected the same city, but its people and conditions had changed over three centuries; his old silver exposed him as one of the vanished youths, and the news brought the townspeople to the cave.
rows.anchor: وهو يظن أنها التي فارقها البارحة لكنه وجد المدينة قد تغيرت بما لا يعهد مثله في يوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The townspeople saw the sign confirming the messenger’s account; the youths soon died, after which polytheists proposed a structure while the monotheists who prevailed proposed a mosque.
rows.anchor: قال المشركون منهم ابنوا عليهم بنيانا ربهم أعلم بهم قال الذين غلبوا على أمرهم وهم الموحدون

rows.speaker: أهل الرواية والتاريخ
rows.claim: Most historians date the story between Jesus and Muḥammad; it is absent from the two Testaments, though some Muslim reports say Quraysh heard it from Jews, while Christians preserved it extensively.
rows.anchor: معظم أهل الرواية والتاريخ على أن القصة وقعت في الفترة بين النبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم وبين المسيح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Christian accounts resemble Ibn Isḥāq’s report from Ibn ʿAbbās in some respects but differ from Muslims on the number of sleepers, whether they had a dog, and the length of their sleep.
rows.anchor: أن المصادر السريانية تذكر عدد أصحاب الكهف ثمانية في حين يذكره المسلمون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author explains the Christian estimate of at most two centuries by identifying the persecutor as Decius and dating the awakening to 425, 437, or 439 CE; he says James of Sarūg first recorded this chronology.
rows.anchor: أن الطاغية الذي كان يجبر الناس على عبادة الأصنام وقد هرب منه الفتية هو دقيوس الملك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although famous among Christians, the Ephesus cave does not fit the Qurʾānic sun directions: those imply a south-facing entrance, whereas this cave’s entrance faces northeast.
rows.anchor: ويلزمه أن يواجه باب الكهف جهة الجنوب، وباب الكهف الذي في إفسوس متجه نحو الشمال الشرقي

rows.speaker: البيضاوي
rows.claim: To reconcile Ephesus with the verse, exegetes measured right and left from inside the cave; al-Bayḍāwī says a door facing Banāt Naʿsh lets seasonal sun rays strike side walls, ventilating the cave without reaching the youths.
rows.anchor: قال البيضاوي في تفسيره إن باب الكهف في مقابلة بنات النعش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī argues that Ephesus actually faces northeast, so sunrise would strike the western side by the entrance and sunset would leave the entrance in shadow; only a strained reading avoids the mismatch.
rows.anchor: شعاع الشمس حينئذ يقع على الجانب الغربي الذي يلي الباب عند طلوعها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that Ephesus lacks a فجوة assumes that فجوة means an elevated area, which is uncertain; the author had taken it to mean an open space.
rows.anchor: وهذا مبني على كون الفجوة بمعنى المرتفع وهو غير مسلم وقد تقدم أنها بمعنى الساحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ephesus has no mosque or comparable structure by the cave, and no inscription or other evidence identifies its many graves as the sleepers’ or proves their long sleep and awakening.
rows.anchor: ولا أثر عند كهف إفسوس من مسجد أو صومعة أو نحوهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Rujayb cave lies near Amman, has a south-facing entrance and openings on the east and west that admit sunlight; its inner space includes a small chamber.
rows.anchor: وباب الكهف يقابل جهة الجنوب وفي داخل الكهف صفة صغيرة تقرب من ثلاثة أمتار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Inside are roughly seven or eight Byzantine-style tombs, faded Greek and Thamudic inscriptions, a red dog image, and decorative markings.
rows.anchor: وفي الغار عدة قبور على هيئة النواويس البيزنطية كأنها ثمانية أو سبعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A Byzantine shrine above the cave was later converted into an Islamic mosque, and another early Muslim mosque stands in the forecourt over a Byzantine church; archaeology dates the shrine to Justin I’s era.
rows.anchor: فوق الغار آثار صومعة بيزنطية تدل النقود والآثار الأخرى المكتشفة فيها على كونها مبنية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After centuries as a ruined, forgotten site, Jordanian excavation uncovered Rujayb; the author considers its archaeological signs and some Muslim reports the strongest fit for the Qurʾānic cave.
rows.anchor: وقامت عدة من الأمارات والشواهد الأثرية على كونه هو كهف أصحاب الكهف المذكورين في القرآن

rows.speaker: ياقوت
rows.claim: Yāqūt identifies al-Raqīm as a village near Amman with a palace of Yazīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik; a poet links al-Raqīm and al-Muwaqqar in a line about visiting Yazīd.
rows.anchor: وذكره ياقوت في معجم البلدان وأن الرقيم اسم قرية بالقرب من عمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Amman stands on the site of Philadelphia, a major and beautiful city before Islam that remained under Roman control from the early second century until the Muslim conquest.
rows.anchor: كانت هي وما والاها تحت استيلاء الروم منذ أوائل القرن الثاني الميلادي حتى فتح المسلمون الأرض المقدسة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other proposed locations include a cave on Mount Qāsiyūn near Damascus, one at Petra, a Scandinavian cave with seven uncorrupted Roman-looking bodies, and a cave near Nakhchivan.
rows.anchor: والكهف الثالث كهف بجبل قاسيون بالقرب من الصالحية بدمشق الشام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No evidence identifies any proposed cave as the Qurʾānic one; the Scandinavian and Caucasus claims conflict with the story’s Roman setting and the limits of Roman power.
rows.anchor: ولا شاهد يشهد على كون شيء من هذه الكهوف هو الكهف المذكور في القرآن الكريم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage returns to the Prophet’s grief that disbelievers reject revelation; since worldly adornment is only a trial and will become barren ground, he should continue conveying the message without distress.
rows.anchor: على عدم إيمانهم بالكتاب النازل عليه وردهم دعوته الحقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the exegetical lexicon, multahad means a refuge or place to turn aside; “the Book of your Lord” may mean the Qurʾān or Preserved Tablet, with the latter fitting “none can change His words” better.
rows.anchor: فالملتحد اسم مكان من الالتحاد بمعنى الميل والمراد بكتاب ربك القرآن أو اللوح المحفوظ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the verse resumes the pre-story argument, “recite” can coordinate with the earlier statement about earthly adornment; the unchanged words and absence of refuge then explain the command.
rows.anchor: رجوع إلى ما قبل القصة وعليه فالأنسب أن يكون قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative construes the verse as an instruction to deliver an unchangeable divine message, since a messenger has no refuge from his sender except in carrying out the mission.
rows.anchor: ويؤيد هذا المعنى قوله في موضع آخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alternative is supported by 72:22–23, where the Prophet says no one can protect him from God and he will find refuge only in conveying God’s messages.
rows.anchor: ويؤيد هذا المعنى قوله في موضع آخر

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Rāghib defines ṣabr as restraint under constraint and, more generally, holding oneself to what reason and religious law require or away from what they forbid.
rows.anchor: والصبر حبس النفس على ما يقتضيه العقل والشرع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s “face” means His beautiful names and attributes through which people address and worship Him; the divine essence itself cannot be directly reached.
rows.anchor: ووجهه تعالى أسماؤه الحسنى وصفاته العليا التي بها يتوجه إليه المتوجهون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seeking God’s active attributes, such as mercy and favor, means seeking to be covered by them and become recipients of mercy, approval, and grace.
rows.anchor: فإنما يريد أن تشمله وتغمره فيتلبس بها نوع تلبس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seeking non-active attributes such as knowledge, power, and majesty means drawing near by taking the humble, weak, and ignorant position appropriate before them.
rows.anchor: يريد أن يضع نفسه موضعا تقتضيه الصفة الإلهية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects interpretations that “His face” means approval, God’s essence through an omitted word, or simply turning toward God and seeking nearness.
rows.anchor: وبذلك يظهر ما في قول بعضهم إن المراد بالوجه هو الرضى والطاعة المرضية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling on God morning and evening is a metonym for continuing devotion, since mornings and evenings recur; interpreting it as the two daily prayers or obligatory prayers is unpersuasive.
rows.anchor: والمراد بدعائهم ربهم بالغداة والعشي الاستمرار على الدعاء والجري عليه دائما

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: The root of “pass beyond” carries the sense of overstepping, so “let not your eyes pass beyond them” means do not leave or overlook the poor believers for worldly adornment.
rows.anchor: أصل معنى العدو كما صرح به الراغب التجاوز وهو المعنى الساري في جميع مشتقاته

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says “pass” implicitly means that the eye shies away or rises above them; without that implication, the wording would need a direct object.
rows.anchor: بتضمين عدا معنى نبا وعلا في قولك نبت عنه عينه وعلت عنه عينه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s making a person heedless is punitive forgetfulness after stubborn opposition to truth, parallel to the later image of coverings on hearts and deafness in ears.
rows.anchor: تسليط الغفلة عليه وإنسائه ذكر الله سبحانه على سبيل المجازاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects treating the verse as proof that God compels people to sin; punitive constraint follows their choices.
rows.anchor: فلا مساغ لقول من قال إن الآية من أدلة جبره تعالى على الكفر والمعصية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Punitive constraint does not negate free choice; only constraint imposed initially would do so.
rows.anchor: الإلجاء مجازاة لا ينافي الاختيار والذي ينافيه هو الإلجاء ابتداء

rows.speaker: المجمع
rows.claim: Al-Majmaʿ glosses faraṭ as exceeding the truth; following desire and excess explain the heedless heart and restate its condition.
rows.anchor: قال في المجمع الفرط التجاوز للحق والخروج عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to tell people that truth is from their Lord continues the Prophet’s duties: recite revelation, remain with poor believers, and simply announce the truth while people choose.
rows.anchor: السياق سياق تعداد وظائف النبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم قبال كفرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Whoever wills, let him believe” is God’s address to the Prophet, not part of the quoted command; it presents a formal choice whose threat is made clear by the prepared punishment.
rows.anchor: من كلامه تعالى يخاطب به نبيه صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم وليس داخلا في مقول القول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fire for wrongdoers explains why the Prophet need not press them: the choice carries its own deterrent and consequence, while benefit or harm returns to them.
rows.anchor: إنا إنما نهيناك عن الأسف وأمرناك أن تكتفي بالتبليغ فقط

rows.speaker: المجمع
rows.claim: Al-Majmaʿ defines sarādiq as an enclosing tent-cloth, muhl as oil dregs or molten copper, murtafaq as a leaning place, and shawā as cooking or ripening.
rows.anchor: السرادق الفسطاط المحيط بما فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the punished people “wrongdoers” rather than “disbelievers” identifies the punishment as due to injustice; 7:45 describes them as those who bar God’s path, distort it, and deny the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: الذين يصدون عن سبيل الله ويبغونها عوجا وهم بالآخرة كافرون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrasing “We do not let the reward of one who does good go to waste” signals divine care; it gives the cause in place of the result, meaning believers will receive their reward.
rows.anchor: ليكون دالا على العناية بهم والشكر لهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because punishment answers wrongdoing while reward answers faith together with good works, the verse implies that faith without righteous action earns no reward and may itself be unjust.
rows.anchor: استفدنا منه أن لا ثواب للإيمان المجرد من صالح العمل بل ربما أشعرت الآية بأنه من الظلم

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: ʿAdn means residence; asāwir are bracelets, with sīwār a Persian loan from dast-wāra; sundus is fine brocade, istabraq thick brocade, and arāʾik couches.
rows.anchor: وذكر الراغب أنه فارسي معرب وأصله دستواره

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report says 18:28 was revealed about Umayya ibn Khalaf, who asked the Prophet to expel poor believers and draw Meccan notables near; it glosses heedlessness as sealing, remembrance as monotheism, desire as shirk, and excess as ignorance.
rows.anchor: نزلت في أميه بن خلف وذلك أنه دعا النبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم إلى أمر

rows.speaker: سلمان
rows.claim: Salman reports that influential converts, including ʿUyayna ibn Badr and al-Aqraʿ ibn Ḥābis, asked the Prophet to remove shabby poor Muslims such as Salman and Abū Dharr; the passage then warned them of fire.
rows.anchor: جاءت المؤلفة قلوبهم إلى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم عيينة بن بدر والأقرع بن حابس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qummī gives a similar report naming only ʿUyayna ibn al-Ḥuṣayn; its Medina setting and related reports conflict with the passage’s Meccan context.
rows.anchor: ولازم الرواية كون الآيتين مدنيتين وعليه روايات أخر تتضمن نظيرة القصة لكن سياق الآيات لا يساعد عليه

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر وأبو عبد الله عليهما السلام
rows.claim: Al-ʿAyyāshī reports that the morning-and-evening calling in 18:28 refers to prayer.
rows.anchor: إنما عنى بها الصلاة

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله عليه السلام
rows.claim: Al-ʿAyyāshī reports that the phrase “whoever wills, let him believe or disbelieve” is a threat.
rows.anchor: قال وعيد

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر عليه السلام
rows.claim: A report from al-Bāqir interprets “the truth is from your Lord” as concerning allegiance to ʿAlī; the author classifies it as an application of the verse.
rows.anchor: في ولاية علي عليه السلام

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم
rows.claim: A report from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī explains the liquid like molten metal as oil dregs; when brought near, facial skin falls into it.
rows.anchor: كعكر الزيت فإذا قرب إليه سقطت فروة وجهه فيه

rows.speaker: القمي
rows.claim: Al-Qummī glosses muhl as the sediment left at the bottom of oil.
rows.anchor: المهل الذي يبقى في أصل الزيت

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله عليه السلام
rows.claim: Ibn Sinān reports al-Ṣādiq’s reminder that humans are hollow and need food and drink, linking it to the drink that scorches faces in 18:29.
rows.anchor: خلق أجوف لا بد له من الطعام والشراب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rich man’s expectation that he would receive something better if returned to God rests on imagined personal merit, not divine generosity; he thinks resurrection unlikely but presumes his status guarantees reward.
rows.anchor: مبني على ما تقدم من دعوى كرامة النفس واستحقاق الخير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath particles, emphatic ending, and first-person phrasing expose his self-deception: he says “if I am returned” and “I will surely find,” not that God will return or grant him anything.
rows.anchor: ولم يقل ردني ربي إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The argument echoes 41:50, where a person credits himself for divine favor, doubts the Hour, and presumes he will receive the best from God.
rows.anchor: ولئن أذقناه رحمة منا من بعد ضراء مسته ليقولن هذا لي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believer answers two boasts: the man’s assumed independence over God and his scorn for his companion’s lesser wealth and followers; the reply addresses the first through 18:38 and the second through the later garden comparison.
rows.anchor: وقد حلل الكلام من حيث غرض المتكلم إلى جهتين إحداهما استعلاؤه على الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating that the companion was conversing with him shows his faith and composure remained steady; he speaks gently and avoids insulting the man’s children, only hinting that the garden could fail.
rows.anchor: إشارة إلى أنه لم ينقلب عما كان عليه من سكينة الإيمان ووقاره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Have you disbelieved in the Creator?” condemns the man’s shirk: claiming independence for oneself and worldly causes; that same stance feeds his doubt about resurrection.
rows.anchor: ينكر عليه ما اشتمل عليه كلامه من الشرك بالله سبحانه بدعوى الاستقلال لنفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Against al-Zamakhsharī, the author says the man is not an idol-worshipping polytheist who outright denied resurrection: he calls God “my Lord” and only doubts or deems resurrection unlikely.
rows.anchor: ولو كان كما قال لذكر فيه الإيمان بالمعاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording “if I am returned to my Lord” shows that the man allows the possibility of return; had he categorically denied it, he would have stated the condition without invoking his Lord.
rows.anchor: ولو نفاه لقال ولو رددت ولم يقل ولئن رددت إلى ربي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believer’s response describes the faithful stance in contrast with the wealthy man’s claim; he should have credited the garden to God’s will and denied independent power.
rows.anchor: فينسب الأمر كله إلى مشيئة الله ويقصر القوة فيه تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “What God wills” may mean the thing God willed or that what He wills exists; a conditional reading is possible, but the first best serves the argument that all affairs depend on God.
rows.anchor: والأوفق بسياق الكلام هو أول التقادير لأن الغرض بيان رجوع الأمور إلى مشيئة الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “There is no power except through God” means every created power remains sustained by God and never becomes independent of Him, as 2:165 says all power belongs to God.
rows.anchor: أن القوة لله جميعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believer accepts that he may be poorer and leaves the matter to God, hoping to receive a better garden.
rows.anchor: فلا بأس والأمر في ذلك إلى ربي فعسى ربي أن يؤتيني خيرا من جنتك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He says God may send hail, a scorching wind, lightning, or another heavenly punishment against the garden, or make its water sink beyond reach.
rows.anchor: ويرسل عليها أي على جنتك مرامي من عذابه السماوي كبرد أو ريح سموم أو صاعقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “He was encompassed by its fruit” figuratively means total ruin, like an enemy encircling someone and cutting off every helper; the Qurʾān uses the expression in 10:22.
rows.anchor: الإحاطة بالشيء كناية عن هلاكه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Turning the palms is a gesture of regret; the garden lying collapsed on its trellises depicts complete destruction, whether the root is understood as falling or emptiness.
rows.anchor: كناية عن الندامة فإن النادم كثيرا ما يقلب كفيه ظهرا لبطن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His wish not to have associated anyone with God means he regrets relying on his garden, self, and worldly causes as though they had independent effects.
rows.anchor: ولم أسكن إلى ما سكنت إليه واغتررت به من نفسي وسائر الأسباب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The companion’s words verbally correct the man’s claims, while the garden’s ruin demonstrates the error in expecting worldly permanence, trusting wealth and followers, and claiming self-sufficiency.
rows.anchor: بيانا قوليا لخطأ الرجل في كفره وشركه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-wilāya is commonly read with fatḥa; a kasra reading is also reported with the same sense, while assigning support to fatḥa and sovereignty to kasra is unproven.
rows.anchor: بفتح الواو وقرئ بكسرها والمعنى واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ḥaqq is also reportedly read in the genitive, without established proof; thawāb means outcome or recompense, usually good reward, and ʿuqb means the final outcome.
rows.anchor: والثواب مطلق التبعة والأجر وغلب في الأجر الحسن الجميل

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: Other exegetes take “there” as the time or place of the garden’s destruction and wilāya as God’s rescue when worldly supports fail; the author grants this is true but says it misses the argument.
rows.anchor: في ذلك الموضع أو في ذلك الوقت وهو موضع الإهلاك ووقته الولاية لله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers wilāya as ownership and governance: once worldly causes fail, God alone truly directs people and all things; apparent causes have no independent effect unless God grants it.
rows.anchor: الحق والله أعلم أن الولاية بمعنى مالكية التدبير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is the true, independent reality; other supposed partners are false in themselves and operate only by His permission, so God gives real reward and a lasting outcome unlike transient causes.
rows.anchor: الأسباب الظاهرية المدعوة شركاء له في التدبير والتأثير باطل في نفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is better in reward and outcome because His reality endures, while worldly adornments fade; since people need something to rely on for their affairs, their Lord is better.
rows.anchor: لأنه سبحانه هو الحق الثابت الذي لا يفنى ولا يزول

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some interpret “there” as the Day of Resurrection, with the reward and outcome referring to that day.
rows.anchor: إلى يوم القيامة فيكون المراد بالثواب والعقب ما في ذلك اليوم

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: The second parable depicts worldly life’s quickly vanishing beauty; hashīm is fragile vegetation broken to pieces, and dharw means scattering, though one gloss says bringing it and taking it away.
rows.anchor: والهشيم فعيل بمعنى مفعول من الهشم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rain makes the earth’s plants fresh and beautiful, then they become broken fragments scattered by winds, illustrating how worldly adornment quickly vanishes.
rows.anchor: فصار بعد ذلك هشيما مكسرا متقطعا تعبث به الرياح تفرقه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saying the rain “mixed with it” emphasizes water’s role in forming vegetation; rain is named because other water sources begin with it, and “became” does not restrict the change to morning.
rows.anchor: إشارة إلى غلبته في تكوين النبات على سائر أجزائه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wealth and children are alluring but transient and cannot fulfill most hopes; this conclusion returns to the opening claim that earthly things were made as adornment.
rows.anchor: لكنها زينة سريعة الزوال غارة لا يسعها أن تثيبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “The lasting good deeds” are righteous acts preserved by God; they bring better reward and truer hope because divine mercy and honor are attainable, unlike worldly hopes that mostly deceive.
rows.anchor: المراد بالباقيات الصالحات الأعمال الصالحة فإن أعمال الإنسان محفوظة له عند الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports from the Prophet and the Imams identify the lasting good deeds as the four glorifications, prayer, or love of the Prophet’s family; the author treats these as applications to instances.
rows.anchor: أن الباقيات الصالحات التسبيحات الأربع سبحان الله والحمد لله ولا إله إلا الله والله أكبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These six verses draw a conclusion from the sūrah’s account of worldly seduction, reliance on protectors besides God, spiritual blindness, and bad outcomes, and prepare for the closing declaration at 18:110.
rows.anchor: بيان الآيات الست في منزلة الاستنتاج مما تقدم من آيات السورة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indirect address in “shall We inform you” targets polytheists, made explicit by the later description of those who disbelieved in God’s signs and meeting Him; the plural “deeds” stresses their varied losses.
rows.anchor: ظاهر السياق أن الخطاب للمشركين وهو مسوق سوق الكناية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A person may lose in an undertaking because the effort misses its goal, like a mistaken journey or lost capital; such a loss may be repaired if its cause is recognized.
rows.anchor: إنما يتحقق إذا لم يصب الكسب والسعي غرضه وانتهى إلى نقص في رأس المال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The worst loss is to suffer while believing one profits: unlike an acknowledged mistake, it offers no hope of correction because the person does not see the failure.
rows.anchor: لا يرى غير ذلك وهو أشد الخسران

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who settle in falsehood and mistake it for good are the most hopelessly lost: worldly desires, arrogance, and inherited zeal veil the truth and block its call.
rows.anchor: من جهة انجذاب نفوسهم إلى زينات الدنيا وزخارفها وانغمارهم في الشهوات

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم
rows.claim: A report from ʿUbāda ibn al-Ṣāmit says Paradise has one hundred ranks, each separated by the distance between heaven and earth; Firdaws is highest and the four rivers flow from it.
rows.anchor: الجنة مائه درجة ما بين كل درجتين كما بين السماء والأرض

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله عليه السلام
rows.claim: Al-Qummī reports al-Ṣādiq interpreting the promise of Firdaws as an abode for Abū Dharr, Salmān, al-Miqdād, and ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir.
rows.anchor: نزلت في أبي ذر وسلمان والمقداد وعمار بن ياسر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The named Companions are exemplars rather than the exclusive referents, since the sūrah is Meccan and Salmān believed only in Medina; the author also notes the report’s weak chain.
rows.anchor: وينبغي أن يحمل على الجري أو المراد نزولها في المؤمنين حقا
